hub.description: Decks and fences for Spring Hill, TN homes: HOA review, clay soil, sunny new construction yards, and fenced space for kids and dogs.
hub.intro: Spring Hill grew up fast around the General Motors plant, and most homes here sit in subdivisions that are still fairly new. That shapes almost every deck and fence project in Spring Hill. The backyard is often open sod over graded clay, with a small patio and not much shade. In a lot of households, someone wants the yard fenced for kids or a dog. Before anything gets built, an HOA tends to want a look at the plans.

sections.heading: What a typical Spring Hill backyard looks like
paragraphs: On many newer Spring Hill lots, the builder left a small patio or a basic deck off the back door, then laid sod over graded clay. Trees tend to be young or missing. Houses sit close together, and a drainage swale may run along the back or side lot line. None of that stops a project, but it changes where posts can go and where a gate or stair should land.

Not every part of town fits that picture. Toward the edges of Spring Hill there are older homes on bigger lots and some open farmland, where a fence can run a long way over rougher ground. The city also crosses the line between Maury County and Williamson County, and that matters when it is time to sort out permits, which we cover below.

sections.heading: Decks for newer Spring Hill houses
paragraphs: Plenty of deck projects in Spring Hill start with a back door that sits several steps above the yard and a patio too small for a table. A deck off that door gives you a level spot to eat outside and keep an eye on the kids in the grass. Sun is the other thing to plan for. With few mature trees in many subdivisions, a west facing deck can get very hot by late afternoon, so board color and shade deserve thought early.

The ground under a new yard needs attention too. Clay and compacted fill are common in Spring Hill subdivisions, and footings have to be dug with that in mind. Our page for a [deck builder in Spring Hill](/deck-builder-spring-hill-tn/) goes deeper on how footings are handled in this soil and how a deck plan gets through HOA review.

sections.heading: Fences for kids and dogs in Spring Hill
paragraphs: Spring Hill has a lot of young families, and a fenced yard for children and pets is often the reason people here start pricing a fence. For that job, the fence needs to sit close to the ground with no gaps a small dog can slip through. The gate latch should close on its own every time. Privacy matters too, since many lots look straight into the next yard.

Fence style and height are controlled by covenants in most newer Spring Hill subdivisions, and some also set color or which side faces out. Getting the design approved before any posts go in saves you from tearing a fence out later. The [Spring Hill fence company page](/fence-company-spring-hill-tn/) covers HOA rules and property lines in more detail.

sections.heading: HOA approval usually comes first
paragraphs: For many Spring Hill homeowners, the HOA review is what sets the start date, not the build. Architectural committees usually want a drawing or a copy of the plat showing where the deck or fence will go, along with the material and color you plan to use. Some committees meet on a set schedule, so a request that misses one meeting waits for the next. Our guide to [getting HOA approval for a fence or deck](/guides/hoa-approval-deck-fence/) walks through a clean submission.

Read your own covenants before you fall for a particular style. Rules differ from one Spring Hill neighborhood to the next, and sometimes between sections of the same development. Whether you live in Wades Grove or a smaller subdivision, the documents that apply are the ones recorded for your lot. A fence a friend got approved across town tells you little about what your own board will accept.

sections.heading: Permits, county lines, and marking utilities
paragraphs: Because Spring Hill spans two counties, people are often unsure who handles permits. For property inside city limits, start with the City of Spring Hill codes office, whichever county your lot is in. If your mailing address says Spring Hill but you live outside city limits, the county is usually the one to call. Most attached or raised decks need a permit. Fence rules vary more, so ask before work starts.

Before a single post hole is dug, buried lines have to be marked through Tennessee 811. Newer Spring Hill subdivisions usually run power and communication lines underground, and the green utility boxes near the back corners of many lots show roughly where they go. The boxes do not show the exact path, so the marks matter. Hitting a live line can hurt someone and cut service to the whole street. Make the request early, since it has to happen before the first post hole on any fence or deck.

faqs.q: Should I build the deck or the fence first in Spring Hill?
faqs.a: It helps to plan both together, even if they get built in different years. A fence that ends at a deck corner needs a post in the right place, and deck stairs should lead toward a gate instead of a blank run of fence. Putting both on one drawing also means one HOA request instead of two. If the budget covers only one right now, say what comes next so the first project leaves room for it.

faqs.q: Does it matter if my Spring Hill home is in Maury County or Williamson County?
faqs.a: For a deck or fence inside city limits, the city codes office is usually the first call either way, so the county line matters less than people expect. It matters more if you live outside city limits, where the county sets the rules. Your property tax bill or deed shows which county you are in. When in doubt, call the city with your address and ask.

faqs.q: What should I have ready before asking for an estimate?
faqs.a: A copy of your plat or survey is the most useful thing, since it shows lot lines and easements. Pull your HOA covenants and any architectural guidelines too. Photos of the back of the house and the yard help, along with a rough idea of what you want the space to do. Send what you have through the [estimate form](#estimate) and we can start from there.

deck.description: Deck builder for Spring Hill, TN homes: footings in clay and graded fill, HOA review, city permits, and decks for sunny new construction lots.
deck.intro: A lot of Spring Hill houses were finished with a short set of steps off the back door and a concrete pad that barely fits two chairs. That pad is where many deck conversations here begin. The yard behind it tends to get full sun, and an HOA usually has a say in what gets built. Under the sod, the soil is often clay or fill left from grading. A good deck builder plans around those conditions before the first footing goes in, and this page covers what we look at on Spring Hill lots.

sections.heading: Replacing a builder deck or patio in Spring Hill
paragraphs: Many new homes in Spring Hill came with a small builder deck or a bare slab outside the back door. Some builder decks were framed with little margin, and after a few summers they can show loose railings or boards that cup and split. Adding onto framing like that is often more trouble than it is worth. Taking the old deck off and starting with a fresh layout is often the cleaner path, and it lets you pick the size and shape you actually need.

Think about how you will use the space before you think about boards. A table that seats the whole family takes more room than most builder decks give you. The grill should sit where smoke drifts away from the kitchen door. Consider where the kids will come up from the yard and where a gate to a future fence might go, because those paths decide where the stairs belong.

sections.heading: Footings in Spring Hill clay and graded fill
paragraphs: Much of the ground around Spring Hill is heavy clay, and limestone often sits not far below it, as it does in many parts of Middle Tennessee. New construction lots add another layer: fill that was pushed around when the subdivision was graded. Fill can keep settling for a while after the house goes up. Footings need to bear on firm soil that has not been disturbed, so the depth of each hole depends on local code and on what the digging turns up.

Clay tends to swell when wet and shrink as it dries in late summer. Posts in poorly drained clay can shift, and water pooling at the base of a post speeds up rot. Before laying out post locations, check where your gutters empty and which way the yard sheds water after a hard rain. Sometimes moving a downspout does more for the life of a deck than any upgrade to the boards.

sections.heading: Sun and heat on open Spring Hill lots
paragraphs: In many Spring Hill subdivisions the trees are still small, so a new deck may sit in direct sun for most of the day. Afternoon sun on a west facing deck is the hardest on people and on boards. Dark boards can get uncomfortably hot under bare feet, and that is true of many composite products as well as stained wood. Lighter colors help. Planning for shade from the start helps more, whether that comes from an umbrella or from trees you plant now.

Wood and composite both have a place here. Pressure treated pine costs less up front and takes stain well once it has dried, but it needs cleaning and a fresh coat of sealer every so often to slow graying and cracking in strong sun. Composite asks for less upkeep and does not splinter, though it costs more and darker colors hold heat. Our guide comparing [wood vs composite decking](/guides/wood-vs-composite-decking/) lays out the tradeoffs plainly.

sections.heading: Attaching a deck to a newer house
paragraphs: Many decks are tied to the house with a ledger board bolted to the floor framing. How that ledger is flashed decides whether water stays out of the wall and the rim joist. Vinyl siding and brick call for different details. On brick veneer, a deck usually cannot hang from the wall at all, so it stands on its own row of posts next to the house instead.

Height changes the job too. Some Spring Hill homes sit on lots that fall away toward the back, which puts the door well above grade. A deck at that height needs taller posts with proper bracing and a longer run of stairs, often with a landing. Any deck builder you talk to should be able to explain how the frame will be braced and where the stairs will come down before you sign anything.

sections.heading: HOA review and permits for a Spring Hill deck
paragraphs: Many newer Spring Hill neighborhoods require architectural approval before a deck goes up. Committees often care most about placement and railing style, and some want stain or board color to match the trim. Brixworth and Wades Grove each have their own covenants, so work from the documents for your lot, not a neighbor's. Submit early with a simple drawing. HOA approval is separate from a building permit, and many decks need both.

Inside city limits, permits generally go through the City of Spring Hill, even though the city crosses from Maury County into Williamson County. Attached decks and raised decks usually need a permit and inspections as the work goes along. Rules change, so confirm with the codes office for your address. The guide to [deck permits in Tennessee](/guides/deck-permits-tennessee/) explains how the process tends to work and why skipping it can cause trouble when you sell.

sections.heading: Planning a deck for a busy family yard
paragraphs: With so many young families in town, safety details matter on a lot of decks. Railings need tight baluster spacing so small children cannot slip through, and vertical balusters give a climber less to step on than horizontal ones. Stairs should have a solid handrail and treads that do not get slick in the rain. A gate at the top of the stairs keeps toddlers from wandering down and the dog from coming up. Details like these are much harder to add after the deck is done.

Think about the space under and around the deck as well. A low deck on a flat lot can trap leaves and moisture underneath, while a taller one leaves room for storage or a shady spot for the dog. If a fence is coming later, plan where it meets the deck so the posts line up. The [Spring Hill fence page](/fence-company-spring-hill-tn/) covers the fence side of that plan.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to build a deck in Spring Hill?
faqs.a: Most attached decks and decks raised off the ground need a building permit, and inside city limits that usually means the City of Spring Hill codes office. Low freestanding platforms are sometimes treated differently, but do not assume yours is exempt. Call with your address and a rough description of the deck. If your home is outside city limits, the county usually handles it.

faqs.q: Will my HOA need to approve a new deck?
faqs.a: In most newer Spring Hill subdivisions, yes. Check your covenants and architectural guidelines, which usually spell out what needs review. Expect to submit a drawing that shows the size and location of the deck on the lot, plus the material and color. Committees sometimes meet only on a set schedule, so leave time. Nobody should start building until the approval is in writing.

faqs.q: Is it worth replacing the small deck the builder put on my house?
faqs.a: Often, yes. An addition has to tie into the old frame, and framing sized for a small platform was not meant to carry more. A new layout can be sized for a table and a grill, with stairs where you actually walk. Check whether any existing footings are sound and in a useful spot, but expect to need new ones. Get HOA approval for the new design first.

faqs.q: What decking holds up best in full sun?
faqs.a: No board is immune to Tennessee sun. Wood needs regular cleaning and a fresh coat of stain or sealer to slow graying and cracking. Composite usually holds its color better and needs less upkeep, but darker colors get hot underfoot on an open lot. On Spring Hill yards with young trees, a lighter color and a plan for shade matter about as much as the material itself.

faqs.q: Can a deck go in a yard that slopes toward a drainage swale?
faqs.a: Usually, yes, as long as the deck does not block the path water takes across the lot. Footings should stay out of the low spot where water collects, and nothing should dam the swale. Many Spring Hill subdivisions have drainage easements along lot lines, and the HOA or the city may limit what goes in them. Your plat shows where those easements are, so keep it handy while you plan.

fence.description: Fence installation in Spring Hill, TN: HOA approved styles, privacy fences, dog safe gates, and lot lines on newer subdivision yards.
fence.intro: In Spring Hill, a fence usually has two jobs. It has to keep kids and dogs in the backyard, and it has to get through an HOA review that often controls style and height. Most yards here sit on newer lots with neighbors close on every side and ground that was graded not long ago. Good fence installation starts with those conditions, not with a catalog of styles. Here is what matters on a Spring Hill lot.

sections.heading: What Spring Hill HOAs usually ask of a fence
paragraphs: Most newer subdivisions in Spring Hill have written rules for fences. The rules usually cover height and style, and many also list approved materials or stain colors. It is common to require the finished side to face out toward the neighbors and the street. Some covenants keep fences behind the front corners of the house. A few only allow an open style, such as ornamental metal, on lots that back up to common space.

Get the covenants for your lot before you settle on a design. Campbell Station has its own, and so does nearly every newer subdivision in town. The architectural committee has the final say, and a fence built without approval may have to come down. Committees typically ask for the fence line drawn on your plat, plus the style and color. Any fence company you hire should see the approval letter before the first post hole is dug.

sections.heading: Fencing for kids and dogs in Spring Hill yards
paragraphs: Keeping the dog home is a big reason many Spring Hill families look into a fence. What works depends on the dog. Jumpers need height. Climbers use the horizontal rails as a ladder, and an HOA rule that puts the finished side out leaves those rails facing your yard, so pick the style with the dog in mind. Diggers are the hardest to stop, and the soft topsoil spread over many new construction yards does not slow them down much. A fence for small children follows similar rules, with extra attention on gates.

Closing the gap at the bottom matters as much as height. On uneven ground, boards should follow the grade closely so no low spots open up between posts. Gates are the weak point in most dog fences. A self closing hinge and a latch that catches every time keep a gate from being left open by a kid in a hurry. Our guide to the [best fence for dogs](/guides/best-fence-for-dogs/) goes further.

sections.heading: Property lines, easements, and 811 on newer lots
paragraphs: Newer Spring Hill lots usually come with a recorded plat, and some homeowners also got a survey at closing. That is a good start, but corner pins sometimes get buried or knocked loose during construction and landscaping. If there is any doubt about the line, locating the pins or ordering a new survey usually costs less than moving a fence. Talk with the neighbor as well, especially if they already have a fence you might tie into.

The plat also shows easements. Drainage easements along rear and side lot lines are common in subdivisions here, and a fence across a swale can back water up into your yard or a neighbor's. Utility easements matter too, since a utility may need access and a fence inside one could have to come down. Before any digging, buried lines get marked through Tennessee 811. Our guide on [fences and property lines in Tennessee](/guides/fence-property-line-tennessee/) covers the rest.

sections.heading: Setting posts in clay, rock, and fill
paragraphs: Posts carry the whole fence. In a newer Spring Hill yard, an auger may pass through a thin layer of topsoil, then compacted clay, and sometimes buried rock or construction debris left from grading. Limestone is common under the soil in this part of Tennessee, and hitting it can slow a job down or call for heavier tools. Near the house, loose backfill may need a deeper hole to reach firm ground.

Water is the other thing that ruins posts. Clay holds moisture, and a wood post in a wet hole can rot at the ground line while the pickets still look fine. Posts rated for ground contact, set in concrete with the top shaped to shed water, tend to last longer. It is one reason some cedar fences are built on pressure treated posts: the pickets can be cedar, but the part in the ground needs the ground contact rating.

sections.heading: Privacy fence styles that fit a Spring Hill subdivision
paragraphs: With houses this close together, a privacy fence is often the first choice for a Spring Hill backyard. Board on board gives full coverage because the boards overlap. Shadowbox alternates boards on each side of the rails, so it looks the same from both sides, and the small gaps between boards let wind through while blocking a straight view. Horizontal slat designs show up in some newer neighborhoods, though not every HOA allows them. Our [privacy fence options](/guides/privacy-fence-options/) guide compares them side by side.

Material comes down to budget and upkeep. Pressure treated pine is the common choice, and it takes stain well once it has dried out. Cedar costs more but usually stays straighter as it weathers. Vinyl needs very little upkeep, and some HOAs allow it while others do not. Whatever you pick, check the approved list first so the fence installation is not held up waiting on a second review.

sections.heading: Gates, slopes, and where the fence meets the deck
paragraphs: Plan gates around how you use the yard. A mower gate should be wide enough for your mower with some room to spare, and it helps to put one on the side where you keep the trash cans. Some Spring Hill lots slope gently toward a swale at the back, and the fence has to follow that grade. Stepped panels leave a triangle gap under each step, which matters with a small dog. Racked panels tilt to follow the ground and keep the bottom closer to it.

If you have a deck or plan to add one, think about how the two meet. A fence that ends at a deck post, or a gate at the bottom of the deck stairs, has to be laid out with the deck in mind. Putting both on one drawing makes the HOA request cleaner as well. Our page on hiring a [deck builder in Spring Hill](/deck-builder-spring-hill-tn/) covers the deck side of the plan.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for a fence in Spring Hill?
faqs.a: It depends on where you live and what you are building. Some Tennessee cities require a fence permit, while others only expect you to follow zoning rules on height and placement. Call the City of Spring Hill codes office with your address before work starts, or the county if you live outside city limits. HOA approval is a separate step either way, and it is often the stricter one.

faqs.q: How tall can a privacy fence be in a Spring Hill subdivision?
faqs.a: There is no single answer. City zoning may limit fence height, and many HOAs add their own rules, often allowing less height near the street than in the backyard. Whichever rule is stricter is the one you have to follow. Check your covenants and ask the codes office before choosing panels, since height is usually the first thing a committee looks at on a privacy fence request.

faqs.q: Can I tie my new fence into my neighbor's existing fence?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Tying in saves a run of posts, but it needs the neighbor's permission, and the two fences should be close in height and style or the HOA may object. The shared posts also belong to someone, which matters when one side needs work later. A common alternative is to set your own posts just inside your line so each fence stands on its own.

faqs.q: How do I keep a small dog from squeezing under the fence?
faqs.a: Keep the bottom close to the ground along the whole run. On a sloped or lumpy yard, that takes some grading and posts set to follow the ground. A rot resistant board along the bottom closes most small gaps, and a buried wire apron helps with diggers. Check the space under each gate too, since gates are a common escape route for small dogs.

faqs.q: Should the finished side of my fence face in or out?
faqs.a: Many Spring Hill HOAs require the finished side to face out, toward neighbors and the street, which leaves the posts and rails on your side. Even where it is not required, facing the good side out is the more neighborly choice. If you want a clean look from both sides, a shadowbox style solves that, since the boards alternate on each side of the rails.
